title: Cattle and Traditional Livelihood
subtitle: The importance of cattle, farming, seasonal movement, and the natural environment in Murle economic and cultural life
body: Traditional Murle livelihood has been shaped by the environment of the Boma highlands, the Pibor lowlands, river systems, grasslands, forests, and seasonal rainfall. The Murle have historically combined different economic activities rather than depending on only one source of food or wealth. These activities include cattle keeping, cultivation, fishing in suitable areas, hunting in earlier periods, gathering wild foods, trade, and the use of local environmental knowledge.

Cattle have an important economic, social, and cultural place in many Murle communities, particularly among lowland agro-pastoralist populations. Cattle provide milk, meat, and wealth, while herding creates knowledge of pasture, water, animal health, weather, and seasonal movement. Cattle are also connected to family relationships, marriage arrangements, social standing, ceremonies, and obligations between households. Their importance therefore goes beyond their value as ordinary property.

Cattle keeping requires detailed knowledge of the landscape. Herd owners and herders must understand where grass is available, which water sources remain usable during dry periods, where animals can find shade, and how seasonal floods affect movement. Rivers, wetlands, plains, wooded areas, and higher ground all have different uses during the year. This knowledge is passed from experienced people to younger generations through practical participation and observation.

The Pibor and Lotilla plains have historically supported cattle-based livelihoods because of their grasslands, seasonal water sources, and movement routes. During the rainy season, pasture may become more widely available, while the dry season requires careful movement toward reliable water and grazing areas. Seasonal mobility is not simply wandering without direction. It is a planned response to rainfall, pasture conditions, animal needs, disease risks, and the changing availability of natural resources.

The Boma highlands have different ecological conditions from the lowlands. Highland Murle communities have historically placed greater emphasis on cultivation because of the suitability of certain areas for farming. Crops and farming practices vary according to soil, rainfall, altitude, household resources, and local knowledge. The difference between highland and lowland livelihoods should not be treated as a division between separate peoples. It reflects the ability of Murle communities to adapt their economy to different environments within their homeland.

Agriculture provides an important source of food and security for many Murle households. Farming may include the cultivation of grains and other crops suited to local conditions. Agricultural work involves preparing land, planting, weeding, protecting crops, harvesting, storing food, and sharing labour. Farming is strongly affected by rainfall, pests, insecurity, access to tools, and the availability of suitable land. A successful harvest can support a household for months, while a failed harvest can create serious hardship.

Many households combine farming with livestock keeping. This mixed system reduces dependence on one activity and allows families to use different resources throughout the year. Crops provide food for people, while livestock provide milk, wealth, and other products. Animals may also contribute manure that improves soil fertility. The balance between cultivation and herding differs from one locality to another depending on ecology, household size, security, and access to land and water.

Livestock ownership is also connected to social identity and responsibility. Cattle require care from several people, including experienced herders and younger members of the household or community. Children and young people may learn animal behaviour, grazing practices, watering, milking, and protection of herds through participation. This practical education teaches patience, alertness, cooperation, and responsibility for living creatures.

Cattle can serve as a form of stored wealth in an economy where access to cash may be limited. A household with livestock may be able to respond to emergencies, support relatives, arrange important family obligations, or exchange animals for other necessities. However, livestock wealth is not equally distributed, and cattle ownership does not guarantee security. Drought, disease, theft, conflict, market changes, and loss of grazing access can reduce herds and place families under pressure.

Milk has traditionally been an important part of pastoral and agro-pastoral diets. It can be consumed fresh or processed depending on local practice and available resources. Milk production depends on animal health, pasture, water, season, and the type of cattle being kept. The care of milk-producing animals often involves household cooperation, particularly among women and other family members involved in milking, processing, and food preparation.

The natural environment is treated as a resource that must be understood rather than used carelessly. Murle environmental knowledge includes identifying edible plants, medicinal plants, useful trees, wild fruits, water sources, animal habitats, and signs of changing weather. Forests and grasslands can provide food, building materials, firewood, shade, tools, and shelter. This knowledge has historically helped communities survive in areas where modern services and markets are limited.

Fishing has been practiced in areas where rivers, wetlands, and seasonal water bodies provide suitable conditions. Fish can supplement household food supplies and provide an additional livelihood during particular seasons. Fishing knowledge includes understanding water levels, fish habitats, equipment, timing, and local environmental changes. Its importance varies depending on the location of each community and the availability of accessible water resources.

Hunting and gathering were also part of earlier livelihood systems and remain present in limited or changing forms in some areas. Wild foods, fruits, roots, honey, and other natural products have historically supplemented cultivated and livestock-based food. These activities required detailed knowledge of seasons, animal behaviour, vegetation, and safe movement through the environment. Modern changes, population growth, environmental pressure, and restrictions on wildlife have altered the place of hunting in many communities.

Traditional livelihood depends heavily on cooperation. Herding, farming, house construction, food production, migration, and responding to emergencies often require more labour than one person can provide. Relatives and neighbours may work together during planting, harvesting, animal care, settlement preparation, or recovery after hardship. Cooperation strengthens social relationships and makes it possible for households with limited resources to manage demanding tasks.

Women and men contribute to livelihood in different but interconnected ways. Responsibilities vary between communities and households, but women have traditionally played major roles in food preparation, child care, cultivation, milk processing, household management, gathering, and trade-related activities. Men and boys have often been strongly involved in herding, animal protection, settlement movement, and other physically demanding work. These roles are not completely fixed, and economic change has increasingly created overlapping responsibilities.

Young people gain livelihood knowledge through observation, participation, instruction, and gradual responsibility. A child may first learn simple household tasks before taking on more demanding duties such as herding animals, helping in fields, collecting resources, or assisting relatives. This practical education teaches not only technical skills but also discipline, cooperation, environmental awareness, and the importance of contributing to the household.

Traditional livelihoods have been affected by conflict, displacement, climate variability, cattle disease, insecurity, changing borders, limited markets, and the expansion of towns. Displacement can separate people from grazing areas, farms, fishing sites, tools, livestock, and established trade networks. When families move to towns or camps, they may lose access to the environmental conditions that supported their former way of life. These changes can create food insecurity and weaken the transmission of traditional knowledge.

Climate and environmental change are increasingly important challenges. Irregular rainfall, longer dry periods, flooding, pasture degradation, water shortages, and livestock disease can make traditional livelihood systems more difficult to maintain. Communities respond through movement, adaptation, diversification, and changes in resource use, but their ability to adapt is limited when insecurity or lack of services prevents safe access to land and water.

Modern education, wage employment, markets, mobile phones, transportation, and government services are creating new livelihood opportunities for Murle people. Some families now combine traditional activities with trading, teaching, public service, business, transport, or employment in towns. This does not necessarily mean that traditional livelihood has disappeared. Instead, many households are developing mixed economic strategies that connect rural life with urban and national markets.

Cattle and traditional livelihood remain important because they connect Murle culture to land, seasons, family responsibility, food security, and environmental knowledge. Protecting these livelihoods requires peace, access to grazing and farming land, veterinary services, functioning markets, water infrastructure, education, and respect for local knowledge. The future of Murle livelihood will depend on combining valuable traditional practices with sustainable methods and new opportunities that improve the wellbeing of communities.
